content.title: Cover letter
content.comment:
Dear All,

We are grateful for the referees’ diligent efforts and insightful comments on our paper.
In addition to the detailed responses to each referee’s comment, we would like to further highlight the motivation of our work as well as its impact and significance in the field. 
Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in humans. PD is characterized by the gradual loss of dopaminergic neurons in the Substantia Nigra (a part of the midbrain). At present, the number of dopaminergic neurons in the Substantia Nigra is one of the most important indexes in evaluating drug efficacy in PD animal models. Loss of dopaminergic neurons lead to motor neuron associated dysfunction as observed in PD patients and animal models. Preventing loss of dopaminergic neurons is the most important goal of PD targeting therapies. It is critical to quantify DA neurons hence the ideal machine learning model should be able to identify and detect DA neurons specifically. These neurons are different from other neurons in the brain and therefore we trained the model precisely on DA neurons. Tyrosine Hydroxylase (TH) is an enzyme that is specifically expressed in DA neurons and its level indicates the health status of the neurons. TH staining is used to evaluate the number and phenotypic properties of DA neurons. Currently, analyzing and quantifying dopaminergic neurons is conducted manually by expert biologists through careful analysis of digital pathology images. However, this approach is laborious, time-consuming, and highly subjective, which significantly delays the progress in PD research and drug development. As such, a reliable and unbiased automated system is highly demanded for the quantification of dopaminergic neurons in digital pathology images. To give an example on the impact of this work, we can attest that in a pre-clinical industry setting lab, 12-15 animal studies are conducted in a year which is equal to 750 animals and requires detection of dopaminergic neurons in each animal to evaluate the success or failure of their study. Each animal study requires at-least 2 months to do the task that our developed  model is able to perform in less than 48 hours which includes data preparation and organization. If we amplify this to other industry and academic labs focusing on PD preclinical studies, the impact of this automated approach can be realized. To this end, this paper is the first work to provide a deep learning solution for the automatic segmentation and quantification of dopamine neurons. 
We have tried our best to address the concerns and the feedback that the reviewers have provided. The feedback from reviewers have certainly helped us to improve the quality of this manuscript and make it more comprehensible to the interested scientific audience. 

Data-set and Annotations: The data-set used in this study to train the model consists of multiple animal studies hence it is not one dataset but a combination of several data-sets. 30,000 mouse DA neurons were manually labeled  and quality controlled by expert biologists. The variability in animal studies enabled us to train the model on different background stain and section thickness which leads to input data variability in tissue staining. The model is able to perform its task taking into account all these variables. 

Results: To further prove the ability of the model to detect DA neurons, we have tested the model in a blind data-set (model has never seen any of these images. The correlation between human cell counting, our model and comparison to one of the most accepted cell segmentation models (Cellpose) further highlights the contribution and significance of this model for the task in hand. Figure 4, 5 and Supplementary Fig 1.

Counting numbers and beyond: We have now demonstrated the model’s ability to measure properties of DA neurons beyond the cell count (Figure 6). TH intensity in DA neurons  is an indicator of the health status of the neuron and we are able to categorize the segmented DA neurons based on the TH intensity indicating its health status. This data allows the biologist to understand the loss of DA neurons with a lot more depth than just counting numbers. A compensation mechanism is displayed by DA neurons upon insult and injury which was extremely difficult to be studied with manual labeling. This approach will now allow the biologist to understand the complexities of DA neuronal loss in PD.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a method to segment (and count) dopaminergic neurons in whole-slide pathology images of mouse brains. First, the method uses self-supervised training in two stages, on natural images and on the pathology images, which provides a good starting point for an encoder network. Second, it plugs this encoder into a segmentation architecture, such as U-Net, which is trained on the segmentation task using in-domain data. The paper is showing that when the data is scarce, this training procedure helps to obtain better results than direct training.

The experiments focus on exploring different options for the self-supervised training, in particular using SwAV and Barlow Twins. One experiment explores several combinations of image augmentation for training of the segmenter. Final results are compared against connected components and human performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros
- the paper addresses a clinically relevant task obtaining results almost comparable to human performance

Cons
- i find the baseline used for counting very weak (connected components)
- the paper is limited to segmentation (and counting) of dopaminergic neurons only through the use of the dataset, I do not see any good reason for this and would expect evaluation on other common public datasets (BraTS, ISIC, ...) to add value to the readers
- lack of comparison to other recent biomedical segmentation methods (Attention U-Net, RCA IU-Net, U-Net transformer)
- limited analysis, there is very little to be learned from the paper


BraTS18: https://www.med.upenn.edu/sbia/brats2018.html  
ISIC18: https://challenge2018.isic-archive.com/  
Schlemper et al (2019). Attention gated networks: Learning to leverage salient regions in medical images.  
Punn & Agarwal, RCA-IUnet (2022). a residual cross-spatial attention-guided inception U-Net model for tumor segmentation in breast ultrasound imaging.  
Petit et al (2021). U-net transformer: Self and cross attention for medical image segmentation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I would expect the paper to explore the necessary properties of the pre-training datasets. Is ImageNet-1k big enough? Would the results improve if one uses ImageNet-22k? What would happen if instead of the natural image pre-training dataset, some dataset(s) closer to the target dataset was used (microscopy images) - would the final results improve or degrade?

The paper suggests that self-supervised pre-training is the way to go, but I wonder why it should be preferred over pre-training on a segmentation task, even if using data from a completely different domain, e.g., cityscapes.

I find interpretation of the augmentation search experiment in Sec. 4.5 wrong/misleading in the following:
- the paper says that the experiment reveals that random crop as an augmentation significantly improves performance, I would argue that this is to be expected and fairly common practice
- the paper says that the difference between Mode 4 and 5 demonstrates that elastic deformation has a negative impact, I would argue that it demonstrates that the given implementation of the elastic deformation has a negative impact, not elastic deformation as such

Along similar lines, the discussion of the experiment in Sec. 4.3, seems to discover that pre-training on different datasets brings robustness, but I would argue that is also known.

I would not know how to re-produce the results or benchmark the method as it is not tested on any public dataset.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Even if the paper is well written, from my point of view it is not bringing enough value (see above) to recommend it to be accepted.

Minor improvements:
- "making the representation invariance" -> "making the representation invariant"

content.summary_of_the_paper: The reviewed paper proposes an end-to-end system for the detection, segmentation, and counting of dopaminergic neurons in animal models of Parkinson's disease from pathology images. According to the authors, the main contribution of this work is a self-supervised pre-training strategy that helps the proposed system perform well, despite a limited number of annotated examples. Experiments conducted on a small in-house dataset of pathology images from PD animal models seem to suggest the effectiveness of the proposed end-to-end framework and self-supervised learning strategy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Overall, the paper has a very clear and consistent structure. The reviewer especially appreciated a very simple structure of the experiments and results section, with experimental setup always coming first making reading much less effortful.

On the other hand, to the reviewer's best understanding the main novelty of this work was in applying existing techniques to a novel domain or in other words dataset. As this does not seem to be sufficient, it might have helped if the authors could explain what exactly about segmenting and counting dopaminergic neurons from PD animal models makes it very hard problem and what is even more important different from the rest of the phatology image analysis work that has been performed in the past. Otherwise, this contribution does not sound very significan, i.e. can people who work on let say segmenting cells from other regions in the brain or not associated with PD do the same thing?

Another, aspect that seems to be important is that at the moment paper presents essentially only one data point as a proof that the proposed method works. Although this is understood that the focus of this paper was on dopaminergic neurons, which is not very common type of data, it might have still be an advantage to check if the proposed self-supervised learning strategy works as well on other pathology datasets. This would provide evidence for the strength and the overall utility of the discussed strategies. 

Some parts of the paper hint at certain technical issues. For example in the related works, the authors compared their proposed strategy for pre-training segmentation model with other works done in the field of dopaminergic neurons, which however used object detection. The authors rightfully pointed out that those object detection methods are inferior to their's because former cannot compute morpholical and intensity-based properties of identified cells, while segmentation models can, which can be rather important in the downstream application. Yet, in this work, for some reason, an ability of the model to extract accurate morphology and intensity-based properties was not tested, which leaves the reader wonder if these properties are as important after all. Then, in the results of the first experiment (self-supervised models provide more generalisable representations) the authors claim that in their experiments ImageNet pre-trained model performs worse than randomly initialised model. They explain this observation by saying that there might be a big domain shift, from ImageNet to phatology images, which might be the case. But then it is not clear how this explanation fits the next observation made for using 25% of data instead of 100%. In that case ImageNet pre-trained model suddenly performs much better than randomly initialised one. Also, it would help if the authors could elaborate on the significance of this difference between randomly initialised and ImageNet pre-trained resutls, provided that there are 10 observations, the difference in means is 0.57 and sd for at least one model is 3.37. Could the authors provide the p-value for their hypothesis convincing readers that the difference they observe is significant?

Finally, as already mentioned, the paper is written in a very clear and comprehensive style. However, some legibility aspects can be improved. For examples, all the citations should be provided in brackets e.g. "Instance discrimination methods Zbontar et al. (2021); He et al. (2020); Caron et al. (2021); Grill et al. (2020); Chen & He (2021); Chen et al. (2020) have recently sparked a renaissance in the SSL paradigm" -> "Instance discrimination methods (Zbontar et al., 2021; He et al., 2020; Caron et al., 2021; Grill et al., 2020; Chen & He, 2021; Chen et al., 2020) have recently sparked a renaissance in the SSL paradigm". Otherwise, citations become integral part of the sentence and essentially make the sentence unreadable. 

Also, several important explanations are missing, e.g. the details of how the dataset was annotated, as well as explanations how these annotations are verified to make sure their high quality; how the error rate presented in the section 4.4 was calculated, and why the authors did not show the predicted count of cells along with manually produced; in the case predicted and manually identified cells overlapped at which point this overlap is considered a true positive and at which it is a false negative (what is the value of the threshold);
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity of this work is high and sufficient. Not much needs to be done to improve it besides some extra work with citations and adding missing details as described in the previous section. 

The quality of this work can significantly be improved by adding more datasets and addressing technical concerns listed in the previous section. 

At present the novelty of this work is unclear. There is nothing that really comes to mind besides applying a set of existing methods to a relatively novel domain. As described in the previous section, more explanation is necessary to clarify the novelty of this work. 

Reproducibility is limited because the only dataset that was used in this work is not made public.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, the reviewed paper has a very clear structure with a very plain set of contributions. Yet, a compendium of various worries including an unclear novelty, limited evidence presented in the paper, and several technical issues prevent this reviewer from recommending acceptance.

This reviewer is looking forward to the rebuttal, hoping that they have missed something important, and are happy to be corrected by the authors. In either case, the reviewer wishes the authors the best of luck with this paper and wants to signal optimism about the future of this work.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: They use a cross-domain self-supervised pre-training approach to exploit the power of unlabeled natural and medical images for representation learning.

Weakness: there are many self-supervised approaches for segmentation but the authors only consider one architecture and apply it to their domain (i.e. Parkinson's disease). So novelty is limited for ICLR conference.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
In Table 3b, the author only compares the naive approach of counting cells but there are many DL-based segmentation approaches in digital pathology so it needs to be compared with other approaches. 

4.5. ablation experiments: these data augmentation techniques are standard techniques so this reviewer is wondering why the author claims these are ablation experiments. 

Typically digital pathology images (immunohistochemistry) show variations in staining quality. This reviewer wonders how they solve this issue as it will be important for the generalization of the proposed approaches.

In Figure 2, the approach only detect positively stained cells in immunohistochemistry images. This reviewer is wondering how they train only positive cell segmentation (not segmenting other cells, i.e., Figure 2 Hematoxilyn only stained cells).
content.summary_of_the_review:
The authors propose an end-to-end deep learning framework for segmenting and quantifying dopaminergic neurons in PD animal models. Their framework relies on self-supervised learning advances to handle the limited data for training deep models. They show the effectiveness of the developed method in quantifying neurons with a small amount of labeled data. 

The authors show a model comparison with pre-training data on self-supervised learning settings and different augmentation techniques. However, it would be good to compare it with the other existing segmentation models in digital pathology applications.

content.title: Self-supervised Learning for Cell Segmentation and Quantification in Digital Pathology Images
content.abstract: Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in humans, impacting 2-3% of people over the age of 65. PD is characterized by the gradual loss of dopaminergic neurons in the Substantia Nigra (a part of the midbrain). At present, the number of dopaminergic neurons in the Substantia Nigra is one of the most important indexes in evaluating drug efficacy in PD animal models. Currently, analyzing and quantifying dopaminergic neurons is con- ducted manually by expert biologists through careful analysis of digital pathology images. However, this approach is laborious, time-consuming, and highly subjective, which significantly delays the progress in PD research and drug  development. As such, a reliable and unbiased automated system is highly demanded for the quantification of neurons in digital pathology images. To this end, in this paper, we propose an end-to-end deep learning framework for the segmentation and quantification of dopaminergic neurons in PD animal models. Our framework relies on self-supervised learning advances to handle the limited amount of data for training deep models. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the developed method in quantifying neurons with a small amount of labeled data. As a result, the proposed methodology can lead to reliable data support for PD research and drug discovery by accelerating the digital pathology analysis.
